title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription software was set by default to automatically join meetings linked to workplace calendars and record all participants without explicit notification that the recordings would be used to train its AI model. The company's privacy policy mentioned AI training, but users report not knowing their confidential conversations were being collected for this purpose. A court allowed a class-action lawsuit over these practices to proceed, alleging violation of state and federal wiretapping and privacy laws.

The failure is one of consent and transparency in a system deployed at scale. The software's default behavior recorded private conversations across Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams for machine learning purposes without ensuring participants understood and agreed to this use. Catching this would have required the company to obtain explicit opt-in consent before recording, to notify all meeting participants that recording and training use would occur, and to verify that de-identification actually removed identifying information from sensitive business data before using it for AI training.

Whether the company violated wiretapping laws, whether de-identification was effective, and whether the privacy policy was sufficiently clear are not established by the lawsuit itself.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View tech company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission to train its artificial intelligence transcription service. The suit, led by plaintiff Justin Brewer, claims the company's Otter Notebook tool records Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings by default without notifying participants that their conversations will be shared with Otter for AI improvement purposes. The company's software can automatically join meetings when linked to workplace calendars, recording all participants without their consent. Otter claims to have 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since 2016.

The lawsuit alleges Otter violated state and federal privacy and wiretap laws, arguing that while the company's privacy policy mentions AI training, many users remain unaware their data is being used. Recent complaints on social media have described incidents where confidential business details and conversations with sensitive sources were recorded and transcribed without proper consent. Otter maintains it de-identifies data before using it for machine learning, but the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information. The company has stated it does not share data with foreign governments or law enforcement.
